description: What becomes available when, on the evolutionary time bar (Ga = billions of years ago). Three lists: levels (the discrete jumps of the time bar, each with the date it is played at), features (game mechanics each level unlocks; once unlocked a feature is always the player's choice to use, and some, such as a fixed body size, make the organism easier to maintain), and proteins (when each protein or family existed; the game offers a protein only from available_from_ga). Events are reference dates. Proteins: earliest_ga and latest_ga bound the estimates found (null = not dated); available_from_ga is the conservative date the game uses; certainty: established | likely | debated | assumed (plausible, no dating found) | unverified (to check).

levels.name: The fermenter
levels.summary: One prokaryote in a pH 7.3 sea: adapt its transport proteins and how much it repairs itself. It has one flagellum, which runs at random and drives it over the ground; more flagella cost ATP to build and run.

levels.name: Division
levels.summary: Put energy into growth and storage; divide when a daughter is built, or spend glycogen to finish one. Small prey cells swim past: a cell can engulf them and food packets smaller than itself. Two directions open: multicellularity, so daughters stay and form a colony, and (after swallowing 10 prey cells) mitochondria; a lineage may take either or both. Processing to decide when to swim (planned).

levels.name: Smell
levels.summary: Chemoreceptors let a cell sense the trace species food packets carry, so it can swim towards them (planned).
levels.note: Historically these exist from the game's start: bacterial chemotaxis evolved from two-component systems after the three domains split, well before 2 Ga (Wuichet & Zhulin 2010). Level 3 is a pacing choice.

levels.name: Breathing oxygen
levels.summary: Membrane respiration with heme-copper oxidases where O2 is available (planned).

levels.name: The eukaryotic cell
levels.summary: The eukaryotic cell: the Na+/K+-ATPase and the cytoskeleton arrive (planned). Mitochondria are evolved at level 2.

levels.name: Sticking together
levels.summary: Adhesion lets cells form groups that are adapted separately: the start of organs (planned).

levels.name: Animals
levels.summary: Tissues with collagen and cadherins; a body can hold a fixed size, turning growth energy into replacing damaged and dead cells (planned).

levels_note: Draft level sequence (2026-10-08) for open question 3 in adapting_plan.md; dates follow the protein and event entries below. Each level lasts duration_s of simulated time (level 1: one week, enough to start starving; later levels' durations are placeholders), then the next level begins and the skill window opens.
arrivals_note: What appears in the world per second at each level, constant whatever is already there: food packets (food_per_s; carried_share of them brought by other creatures, the rest lying on the ground and coming into view) and prey cells (prey_per_s, none at level 1; food once a cell engulfs them, level 2), later enemies and friends. A level's regions may override them (regions[].arrivals), to set scarcity or abundance. Calibrated 2026-10-12 with packets at a cell's density (4.9e-15 mol): food 3e-3 packets/s, so an untouched level-1 cell eats 1.69e-13 mol and its ATP runs out on day 4 (the outcome hangs on the gaps between packets: in probes 3e-3 to 3.5e-3 ran out on days 1.5-4 depending on the random sequence, 4e-3 never). Prey 2e-4/s from level 2, so a creature that engulfs swallows about 10 in the level's week only with luck or effort: the untouched creature (starving since level 1) swallows 4 and dies at the end of level 2; a fed cell starting level 2 swallows 7 (other seeds: 11; 6 with 3 flagella). Later levels copy level 2 until tuned.

features.name: Protein expression
features.effect: Expression sliders for the transport proteins and glycolytic enzymes of a cell group; new copies cost ATP to build, and every copy costs ATP to keep. The membrane holds only so many transporters (a ceiling that scales with membrane area).
features.explanation: A cell's abilities are its proteins: transporters in the membrane, enzymes in the cytosol. Each slider sets how many copies the cell keeps of one protein, relative to its starting amount. Making a protein costs about 4 ATP per amino acid (a 300-residue transporter is ~1,200 ATP), and proteins wear out and are replaced, so every copy kept also costs ATP continuously. Transporters sit in the membrane, which has room for only so many: proteins can fill about 15% of its area (the starting cell uses about a third of that room), a limit that grows with the cell's surface. A carrier you evolve later starts at none, and its slider sets the share of that room it takes. More of a transporter moves more of its cargo, but only while the cargo is there to move; at low glucose the cell's uptake is limited by how fast glucose diffuses to it, not by how many carriers it has.

features.name: Repair
features.effect: How much a group spends repairing damage (0-1). Low repair saves energy but cells die when damage reaches a lethal load; the colony then relies on division.
features.explanation: Proteins, membranes and DNA are damaged all the time (oxidation, misfolding, chemical wear). Cells spend energy finding and fixing or replacing damaged parts. Spending less on repair leaves more ATP for growth or movement, but damage then accumulates, and a cell dies once it reaches a lethal load. Bacteria live with this trade-off: fast-growing populations can afford to lose cells because division replaces them, which is why turning repair down can pay off once your cells divide.

features.name: Swimming (flagellum)
features.effect: The cell starts with one flagellum; its motor runs at random (runs and pauses), driving the cell over the ground on the proton motive force. The flagella slider adds more (each costs ATP to build and protons to run). Turn it off to save the energy.
features.explanation: Many bacteria swim with flagella: long helical filaments turned at their base by a rotary motor in the membrane. The motor is not powered by ATP directly but by protons flowing back into the cell through it, about 1,000 per revolution, so swimming spends the proton gradient your H+-ATPase builds with ATP. At this size water is like syrup: a cell stops within a fraction of a micrometre when the motor stops, so it moves only while it pays. Simple bacteria run and tumble at random; steering towards food needs sensing, which comes later.

features.name: Growth and division
features.effect: Put a share of the energy into building a daughter cell (its proteins, RNA, lipids and DNA). Click a cell to divide once the daughter is built.
features.explanation: A cell divides by first building a second copy of almost everything it has: proteins, ribosomal RNA, lipids for a membrane twice the area, and a copy of its DNA. Most of this cost is protein, and a bacterium spends most of its energy budget on growth when food is plentiful. When the daughter's material is complete the cell splits in two by binary fission. Energy put into growth is energy not available for pumping or repair, so a cell that grows too fast on too little food can starve itself.

features.name: Glycogen storage
features.effect: Store glucose as glycogen (2 ATP per glucose, 3 back later). The store is spent automatically when ATP falls, and clicking Divide spends it to finish a daughter that is nearly built (glycogen holds about 1% of a daughter).
features.explanation: Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose that cells use as a store. Storing a glucose costs ATP (about 2, to activate and attach it), and breaking it down later returns it as glucose-phosphate ready for glycolysis, saving the ATP that glycolysis would spend to phosphorylate free glucose. Bacteria build glycogen when food is plentiful and spend it when food runs out. Because a polymer adds hardly any osmotic pressure, a cell can store far more glucose this way than as free sugar.

features.name: Automatic division
features.effect: Cells divide by themselves as soon as a daughter is built.
features.explanation: A cell in this game divides when you tell it to; real bacteria divide automatically once a daughter is complete, controlled by proteins that sense the cell's size and DNA replication. Turning this on lets every cell divide as soon as it can, which grows the colony fastest when food is steady, but divides cells even when holding back would leave them better stocked for lean times.

features.name: Swimming control
features.effect: Processing to decide when to run the flagella (e.g. keep still on food, swim when it runs out). Planned.
features.explanation: Bacteria do not swim blindly forever: signalling proteins change how often the motor reverses or pauses, so a cell can stay where food is and swim when it runs out. In E. coli, a chain of proteins (CheA, CheY and others) passes a phosphate signal to the motor in a fraction of a second. This feature will let you choose rules for when the flagella run. (Planned.)

features.name: Sugar phosphotransferase (PTS)
features.effect: A high-affinity glucose transporter that phosphorylates glucose as it brings it in, paid by one PEP from glycolysis.
features.explanation: The phosphotransferase system (PTS) takes glucose across the membrane and attaches a phosphate to it in the same step, using a phosphate passed along a chain of proteins from phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), an intermediate of glycolysis. Glycolysis would otherwise spend an ATP to phosphorylate free glucose, so the PTS gets glucose in at almost no extra cost, and the fermenter keeps its 2 ATP per glucose. It binds glucose tightly (half-saturated at a few micromolar, compared with millimolar for the starting transporter), so it keeps working when food is scarce. Lactic acid bacteria and E. coli use it for glucose. It is found only in bacteria.

features.name: ABC sugar importer
features.effect: The highest-affinity glucose importer, powered by ATP: about 2 ATP per glucose.
features.explanation: ABC transporters are ATP-powered pumps found in every domain of life, among the oldest protein families. A binding protein outside the membrane catches the sugar at sub-micromolar concentrations and hands it to the pump, which spends two ATP to move it in. That makes it the best scavenger of traces of sugar, but a fermenter makes only 2 ATP per glucose, so importing single glucose this way leaves almost nothing over. In real bacteria ABC importers bring in chains of sugars (oligosaccharides) instead, where one cycle brings in several glucose units for the same cost.

features.name: Proton-coupled sugar symporter
features.effect: Brings glucose in with a proton, driven by the proton gradient the H+-ATPase builds.
features.explanation: Symporters of the major facilitator superfamily (such as GalP and LacY in E. coli) carry a sugar and a proton across the membrane together. The proton flows down the gradient your H+-ATPase builds, which pulls glucose in even against its own gradient, so the cell can take up sugar from medium that holds less than its cytosol. Each glucose costs one proton, roughly a quarter to a third of an ATP to pump back out, and adds to the acid load the cell must remove. Its affinity lies between the starting facilitator and the PTS (tens of micromolar to a millimolar).

features.name: Carbon regulation
features.effect: Cells turn the glucose facilitator down by themselves while other carriers bring glucose in, so it stops leaking glucose back out. Planned.
features.explanation: A facilitator such as Glf only lets glucose run down its gradient. Once a cell pumps glucose in with an active carrier (an ABC importer or a proton symporter), the sugar inside can rise above the sugar outside, and the facilitator then carries it straight back out: the cell pays to bring the same glucose in twice. Bacteria avoid this by regulating which carriers they make, a set of controls called carbon catabolite repression: when a preferred sugar and carrier are working, the genes for the others are switched off and some carriers are blocked directly (inducer exclusion). With this skill your cells cut their Glf expression automatically while active carriers supply them. (Planned.)

features.name: Engulfing
features.effect: A cell that touches a food packet or a prey cell smaller than itself takes it inside, in a vacuole. The cell's surface hydrolase digests it there and the cell's own sugar carriers take the sugar up from the vacuole, so none is lost or shared. What a cell swallows shares one vacuole, which must stay smaller than the cell (food packets always leave room for a prey cell). Prey cells swallowed are counted.
features.explanation: Engulfing (phagocytosis) is how many eukaryotic cells eat: the membrane flows around a particle and closes behind it, leaving it in a vacuole. The vacuole is still outside the cytosol: its membrane faces the food the way the outer membrane faces the sea, so enzymes digest the food in it and transporters carry the sugars across into the cytosol, at the vacuole's high concentration and with nothing lost to the water. At 1.9 billion years ago this is a stretch for a prokaryote-grade cell. Phagocytosis is a eukaryotic trait and is not documented this early. The cultured Asgard archaeon, the closest living relative of the eukaryotes' host cell, makes long membrane protrusions but has not been seen to engulf anything (Imachi et al. 2020); a few modern bacteria do something like it (the planctomycete Candidatus Uab amorphum engulfs other cells; Shiratori et al. 2019). Whether eating by engulfment came before the mitochondrion and made its capture possible ('phagocytosis early') or came after it is debated. The game lets you explore that route.

features.name: Multicellularity
features.effect: Daughters stay attached to the cell that made them, so the creature grows as a colony. Without it each daughter leaves when its parent divides and lives on its own nearby, swimming and eating as your cell does and competing with it for food, but beyond your control: it counts as offspring and earns reproduction points, as do its own daughters and theirs, and the creature stays one cell. A daughter that dies becomes food where it lies. Later colony features (boundary and inner cells, several groups, a fixed body size) need it.
features.explanation: Bacteria that stay stuck together after dividing make chains, filaments and mats; filamentous cyanobacteria were multicellular by about 2.5 to 2.4 billion years ago (Schirrmeister et al. 2015). Staying together lets the cells share the water between them and, later, specialise, and it makes the creature bigger; but every cell then shares the creature's food and fate. In the game it is one of two directions open at level 2, with a single cell that takes in a partner and becomes the start of a eukaryote (mitochondria); a lineage may take both. Without it, every daughter that swims off is offspring (a cell of its own, with its parent's proteins and settings, that may feed, divide and die), and offspring are fitness: the currency evolution counts, since a lineage persists only through the cells it leaves behind. That is why each one earns reproduction points, its daughters' daughters too, and why staying single-celled can pay for a while. A dead cell is food for whoever finds it, its relatives included.

features.name: Mitochondria
features.effect: Available once your cells have swallowed 10 prey cells. A swallowed bacterium that is kept alive inside the cell becomes a partner that later breathes for it. Planned: respiration inside the cell is not modelled yet, so evolving it changes nothing in the cell for now.
features.explanation: Mitochondria descend from an alphaproteobacterium that came to live inside another cell, an archaeon related to today's Asgard archaea, somewhere between about 2 and 1.5 billion years ago: the event behind the eukaryotic cell. How the partner got in is debated. In 'phagocytosis early' views the host already ate by engulfing and one meal survived; in others the two lived side by side, trading metabolites, until the host's protrusions wrapped around the partner (Imachi et al. 2020). Here the route is the first: after swallowing enough prey, one is kept. Each mitochondrion holds its own respiratory membranes, folded inside the cell, so a eukaryote's respiring membrane area is no longer limited to its outer surface; that extra energy paid for larger cells, larger genomes and new machinery such as the cytoskeleton. (Planned: the game does not model respiration yet.)

features.name: Smell (chemoreceptors)
features.effect: Express chemoreceptors to sense the trace species in food packets (aspartate, serine, ribose...); receptors cost protein like any other. Planned.
features.explanation: Bacteria smell their surroundings with chemoreceptors: membrane proteins that bind particular molecules (amino acids such as aspartate and serine, sugars such as ribose) and signal to the flagellar motor. A cell compares the concentration now with a few seconds ago and keeps swimming while things improve, which biases its random walk towards food. Food packets in this game carry trace molecules you can learn to follow. Receptors cost protein like any other. (Planned.)

features.name: Membrane respiration
features.effect: Planned.
features.explanation: Respiration passes electrons from food to oxygen through a chain of membrane proteins that pump protons out; the protons flow back through ATP synthase and make ATP. Fully oxidising glucose this way yields roughly 15 times the ATP of fermenting it to lactate. Oxygen became available in the shallow seas after the Great Oxidation Event (about 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago), and heme-copper oxidases that use it are ancient. Respiration needs membrane area for its proteins, which limits how much a single bacterial cell can do. (Planned.)

features.name: Boundary and inner cells
features.effect: Water between three neighbouring cells becomes a shared space of its own. Cells with part of their edge on open water form the boundary group; cells surrounded by other cells form the inner group. Each group has its own sliders, and cells move between the groups as the colony grows.
features.explanation: By about 1.8 billion years ago bacteria had lived in mats and biofilms for more than 1.5 billion years. In a biofilm, cells sit in a shared, unsealed space between them. Food, waste and acid diffuse through the narrow gaps between cells, so cells on the surface see the sea while cells inside see what their neighbours have left. Gradients form across the colony: in modern biofilms oxygen reaches only 50 to 100 micrometres in, and fermenting biofilms such as dental plaque turn acidic inside. The same cell type can then be in two very different places. Splitting the colony into its boundary and its inside is the first step towards a body with an outside and an inside.

features.name: Extracellular matrix
features.effect: A slider for each group sets how much matrix (a sugar polymer) its cells export into the space between cells. Each glucose unit of matrix costs one glucose and about 3 ATP. The matrix slows diffusion through the gaps and breaks down slowly, returning some glucose. Matrix made where a cell faces open water is lost to the sea.
features.explanation: Biofilm bacteria wrap themselves in extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), mostly polysaccharides. In many biofilms the matrix makes up most of the dry mass, often over 90%, against a few percent for the cells. Making it is costly. Each sugar is phosphorylated and activated as a nucleotide sugar (UDP-glucose or ADP-glucose), polymerised, often on a lipid carrier, and exported. That is about 2 to 4 ATP per sugar unit on top of the sugar itself, and a fermenting cell also loses the 2 ATP it would have made from that glucose. The matrix holds the colony together and slows the diffusion of solutes, keeping what the colony makes and finds near its cells. Its hydrolases also let cells reclaim some of it when food runs short. It is also a public good: neighbours that make none still benefit from it.

features.name: Several cell groups
features.effect: Split cells into groups adapted separately (organs later). Sliders always change every cell in the selected cell's group.
features.explanation: Cells that stick together can specialise: some do one job, others another, as in the heterocysts of filamentous cyanobacteria that fix nitrogen for their neighbours. Splitting your colony into groups lets you adapt each group's proteins and energy use separately. Every slider then changes all the cells of the selected cell's group. This is the start of tissues and organs.

features.name: Fixed body size
features.effect: The group holds its present number of cells: growth energy replaces dead cells instead of adding cells, and goes to repair while the group is full. Easier to maintain; no further growth.
features.explanation: Most animals stop growing at an adult size and from then on spend energy maintaining their body: replacing cells that die and repairing tissues. With this on, a group keeps its present number of cells. Energy that would have made new cells replaces dead ones, and goes to repair while the group is full. A fixed body is easier to keep healthy but no longer grows.

features.name: Regulation
features.effect: Unlocked when your creature first goes half a minute without touching or holding food. A cog beside each expression slider and the growth slider chooses which falling species (ATP, G6P, glucose inside, pH) turn that protein or growth down, so a starving cell spends less.
features.explanation: Real bacteria do not keep spending as if food were plentiful. When energy or carbon runs short they raise a signal molecule, (p)ppGpp, that shuts down the making of ribosomes and slows protein synthesis and growth: the stringent response (Potrykus and Cashel 2008). The genes for ribosomal RNA also read the ATP level directly, so their output falls as ATP falls (Schneider, Gaal and Gourse 2002). Spending less in a famine keeps ATP from running out. That matters because glycolysis has to invest ATP before it pays any back: a cell whose ATP reaches zero cannot restart glycolysis even when food returns. Each cog chooses which falling species turn a protein or growth down. The rule is fixed for now: the target is multiplied by f = C^4/(K^4 + C^4), with K half the species' resting level (for pH, the target falls as the pH drops, half-way 0.3 below rest), so f is 0.94 at rest, 0.5 at half the resting level and near 0 below a quarter. Choose with care: turning down the glycolytic enzymes or the glucose carriers in a famine leaves the cell unable to use food when it comes back, while turning down pumps, exchangers and flagella saves energy it can rebuild later. Experts will be able to choose the function.

achievements.name: First meal
achievements.description: Your creature touched or swallowed food for the first time.

achievements.name: Survived a famine
achievements.description: Your creature went without food long enough to unlock regulation, found food again, and its cells were not starving when it did.

achievements.name: Never starved
achievements.description: A level ended without your creature's cells ever starving: its survival meter stayed full.

achievements.name: First daughter
achievements.description: One of your cells divided for the first time.

achievements.name: Grandmother
achievements.description: A daughter of your creature had a daughter of its own.

achievements.name: First prey
achievements.description: Your creature swallowed its first prey cell.

achievements.name: Ten prey
achievements.description: Your creature has swallowed ten prey cells.

achievements_note: Achievements shown in the level-end window when earned (each once, in the level it is earned). The sim decides when each is earned (FermenterWorld.Achievements.cs); 'reviewed' is set by a human who has checked the text.

events.name: Last universal common ancestor (LUCA)
events.notes: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution: about 4.2 Ga, genome of at least 2.5 Mb.

events.name: Great Oxidation Event
events.notes: Poulton et al. 2021 (Nature): first rise above 1e-5 PAL at ~2.43 Ga, oscillating until permanent at ~2.22 Ga. The deep ocean stays largely anoxic long after.

events.name: AdaptOrDeity begins
events.notes: The evolutionary time bar starts here: a ~2 um prokaryote fermenter in a sea of pH 7.3 (placeholder between Halevy & Bachan 2017's Archean 6.5-7.0 and Phanerozoic 7.5-9.0).

events.name: Last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA)
events.notes: Placeholder date. A 2024 Bristol thesis puts LECA in the early Proterozoic; Betts et al. 2018 date it relative to fossils (their numbers not checked here).

events.name: Crown-group animals (Metazoa)
events.notes: Molecular clocks: Tonian to Cryogenian (about 0.8 to 0.64 Ga); dos Reis et al. 2015 favour the Cryogenian and stress the uncertainty.

proteins.name: Rotary ATP synthase / ATPase (F-, V-, A-type)
proteins.function: Couples ATP synthesis or hydrolysis to Na+ or H+ flow across the membrane
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's only primary pump: the F1Fo ATPase hydrolyses fermentation ATP to pump 10/3 H+ out per ATP, which powers every other gradient. With respiration it runs the other way and makes ATP.
proteins.notes: Present in LUCA (Modjewski et al. 2025). Mulkidjanian et al. 2008 argue the Na+-coupled form is ancestral (hypothesis). Kobayashi 1985: fermenting Enterococcus hirae uses it in hydrolysis mode to regulate cytoplasmic pH. Jiang et al. 2001: E. coli c10 ring, so 10/3 H+ per ATP.

proteins.name: K+ channel, two-transmembrane (KcsA-like)
proteins.function: Passive K+ conductance
proteins.game_role: Passive K+ conductance; the fermenter's K+ path is the Trk entry.
proteins.notes: Loukin et al. 2005 (secondary summary) place K+ channels before the Bacteria/Archaea divergence; not dated in years.

proteins.name: Trk / Ktr K+ uptake transporters
proteins.function: K+ uptake (low affinity, fast), derived from K+ channel pore motifs
proteins.clade: Bacteria and Archaea; Trk1,2 in fungi
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's K+ uptake: a channel-like K+ path driven by the membrane potential (i_leak_K maths).
proteins.notes: Durell et al. 1999: symporters arose from K+ channels by duplication and fusion. Widespread in bacteria today; no date found. Cao et al. 2011: TrkH has a channel-like selectivity filter.

proteins.name: KdpFABC K+-ATPase
proteins.function: ATP-driven high-affinity K+ uptake (P-type ATPase)
proteins.game_role: ATP-driven K+ uptake when K+ is scarce; a prokaryotic alternative to the Na/K pump.
proteins.notes: KdpA derives from 2TM K+ channels. No date found; treated as present in prokaryotes by the game's start.

proteins.name: Na+/K+-ATPase (P2C alpha subunit)
proteins.function: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP; electrogenic
proteins.clade: eukaryotes (fungi, choanoflagellates, animals, some algae and protists)
proteins.game_role: Not in the 2.0 Ga fermenter any more (replaced by the H+-ATPase, NhaA, Trk and KefC). Unlock with eukaryotes (opisthokonts at the latest).
proteins.notes: Saez et al. 2009: the IIC subfamily most likely originated in prokaryotes, and IIC proteins occur in algae, protozoa and fungi; the animal-fungal ancestor had a Na,K-ATPase-like alpha (Blastocladiella, 1998). Not documented as a 3Na/2K pump in prokaryotes. available_from_ga is a placeholder for the opisthokont ancestor (date not checked).

proteins.name: NhaA Na+/H+ antiporter (CPA2 family)
proteins.function: 1 Na+ out for 2 H+ in, electrogenic; driven by the proton motive force
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's Na+ export. It fails above about pH 7.8 outside at -105 mV, so modern seawater (8.1) needs a primary Na+ pump.
proteins.notes: Taglicht et al. 1993: 2 H+ per Na+, independent of pH 7.2-8.1. Not dated.

proteins.name: KefC-type K+/H+ exchanger
proteins.function: 1 K+ out for 1 H+ in, electroneutral
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's K+ export, which lets the membrane sit below E_K.
proteins.notes: Gulati et al. 2024: structure of E. coli KefC, glutathione-gated (mostly closed in vivo); its basal activity stands in for all K+ efflux. Not dated.

proteins.name: Primary Na+ pumps (Na+-NQR, Na+-translocating decarboxylases, Na+-ATPases)
proteins.function: Pump Na+ out directly with redox or decarboxylation energy
proteins.game_role: Evolvable upgrade that keeps Na+ out when the ocean turns alkaline (pH 8.1 today) and NhaA alone fails.
proteins.notes: Mulkidjanian et al. 2008 argue Na+ bioenergetics is ancient. The individual pumps were not dated here.

proteins.name: Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, prokaryotic (CaCA family, e.g. NCX_Mj)
proteins.function: 3 Na+ in, 1 Ca2+ out
proteins.clade: Archaea and Bacteria; NCX in animals
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's Ca2+ extrusion (prokaryotic equivalent of the SN exchanger).
proteins.notes: Liao et al. 2012 (Science): archaeal NCX_Mj from Methanococcus jannaschii exchanges Na+ for Ca2+; Liao et al. 2016 establish 3:1 stoichiometry. Not dated.

proteins.name: Bacterial voltage-gated Na+ channel (NaChBac family)
proteins.function: Voltage-gated Na+ conductance
proteins.game_role: A Na+ conductance for prokaryotic cells (the fermenter's Na+ leak is unspecific).
proteins.notes: Sodium selectivity evolved independently in bacterial and animal channels (Liebeskind et al. 2013). Not dated.

proteins.name: Major facilitator superfamily sugar transporters
proteins.function: Facilitated or H+-coupled sugar uptake
proteins.clade: all domains (MFS); sugar-porter subfamily distribution not checked
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's glucose facilitator (Glf-type).
proteins.notes: MFS is ancient and ubiquitous in bacteria, archaea and eukarya (Pao et al. 1998; Reddy et al. 2012). Glf itself is a Zymomonas protein; its kinetics stand in for an early MFS facilitator.

proteins.name: Sugar-using glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof)
proteins.function: Glucose to pyruvate with net ATP
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's ATP source.
proteins.notes: Modjewski et al. 2025: trunk glycolysis (gluconeogenic direction) in LUCA; glucose-using routes arose later and spread by gene transfer; glycolysis is not universal among prokaryotes. No date for sugar-using glycolysis; assumed present by 2.0 Ga.

proteins.name: Lactate dehydrogenase (fermentative)
proteins.function: Pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+
proteins.game_role: Homolactic fermentation's last step.
proteins.notes: LDH/MDH superfamily from ancient gene duplications (Madern 2002); MDHs span all three domains, LDHs only Bacteria and Eukarya. No absolute date; a bacterial fermenter with LDH at 2.0 Ga is plausible.

proteins.name: Bacterial lactate carriers (LctP family)
proteins.function: H+-coupled lactate uptake; the export route of lactic acid bacteria is not established here
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's lactate exit (its kinetics currently borrow MCT1's Km).
proteins.notes: LldP / LutP are lactate permeases described for uptake. A prokaryotic export carrier for homolactic fermenters needs a source.

proteins.name: Alpha-amylase family glycoside hydrolases (GH13), surface or secreted
proteins.function: Hydrolyse polysaccharide (starch- and glycogen-like alpha-glucans) outside the cytosol into oligosaccharides and glucose
proteins.clade: all domains (GH13 family); surface-anchored and secreted forms in many bacteria
proteins.game_role: The fermenter's surface hydrolase: digests food packets it touches (environment field) and what its cells engulf (vacuoles, level 2).
proteins.notes: Lengths (UniProt, checked 2026-10-12): SusG, the surface lipoprotein alpha-amylase of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, 692 aa (Q8A1G3; signal 1-22, lipidated Cys23); Bacillus subtilis AmyE, secreted, 659 aa (P00691); Klebsiella pneumoniae pullulanase PulA, a surface lipoprotein, 1,090 aa (P07206); Bacillus licheniformis alpha-amylase, secreted, 512 aa (P06278). The model's 700 aa (upstream L_Hydrolase) is SusG-sized. GH13 is spread over all three domains; its age is not dated here (assumed present at 2 Ga).

proteins.name: Photosystem II (oxygenic photosynthesis)
proteins.function: Splits water, releases O2
proteins.game_role: The source of the planet's O2; a later player-evolvable trait (photosynthesis).
proteins.notes: Cardona et al. 2018 argue for an early Archean water-splitting photosystem; geochemical evidence spans 3.7 Ga to the GOE; origin unresolved.

proteins.name: Heme-copper oxygen reductases (aerobic respiration)
proteins.function: Reduce O2 to water at the end of respiratory chains
proteins.game_role: Membrane respiration: the starting fermenter's first big evolvable upgrade (once O2 is available locally).
proteins.notes: Husain et al. 2026: Mesoarchean origin (before the GOE). Trost et al. 2025: arose in the wake of the GOE (~2.4 Ga). Either way present by the game's start.

proteins.name: Chemoreceptors (methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins) with CheA/CheW/CheY
proteins.function: Sense attractants such as aspartate and serine and steer the flagellar motor
proteins.game_role: Smell: sensing the trace species of food packets (level 3, feature chemosensing).
proteins.notes: Wuichet & Zhulin 2010: the chemotaxis system evolved from simpler two-component systems in Bacteria after the domains separated, and was later transferred to Archaea. Not dated in years; assumed present by 2.0 Ga.

proteins.name: Two-component systems (sensor histidine kinase + response regulator)
proteins.function: Sense the environment and switch genes
proteins.game_role: The ancestor of chemotaxis; later, regulated responses (e.g. switch expression with conditions).
proteins.notes: Widespread and modular; whether they were in LUCA is unsettled. Not dated.

proteins.name: Bacterial flagellum (proton-driven rotary motor)
proteins.function: Swimming, powered by the proton motive force
proteins.game_role: Swimming towards food (level 3, feature swimming); costs proton motive force.
proteins.notes: Age not checked; to verify.

proteins.name: Bacterial globins (flavohemoglobins, sensors)
proteins.function: NO detoxification, O2 sensing (not O2 transport)
proteins.game_role: O2 sensing for the sensory cell type.
proteins.notes: Vinogradov and colleagues: all three globin lineages are bacterial in origin; not dated.

proteins.name: Mitochondrion (alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont)
proteins.function: Internalised respiratory membranes: ~30 ATP per glucose
proteins.game_role: Major milestone: lifts the membrane-area energy limit (energy_metabolism mitochondrial version).
proteins.notes: Timing disputed (mitochondria-early vs late). The Bristol thesis allows endosymbiosis in or before the late Archean; latest_ga 1.5 is a placeholder for LECA, to refine.

proteins.name: Actin, tubulin, myosin (eukaryotic cytoskeleton and motors)
proteins.function: Cell shape, motility, contraction
proteins.game_role: Prerequisite for contractile (proto-muscle) cells.
proteins.notes: Widely regarded as present in LECA; not checked against the 2024 consensus review text.

proteins.name: Integrin adhesion complex
proteins.function: Cell-matrix adhesion
proteins.game_role: Multicellular attachment to a matrix.
proteins.notes: Integrin-complex proteins occur in protists near the base of the opisthokonts. available_from_ga is a placeholder.

proteins.name: Cadherins
proteins.function: Cell-cell adhesion
proteins.game_role: Gluing cells into tissues (multicellular body plans).
proteins.notes: King et al. 2008: Monosiga brevicollis has 23 cadherin genes, so cadherins predate animals. Date tied to the choanoflagellate-animal split (placeholder).

proteins.name: Collagen
proteins.function: Extracellular matrix, tensile strength
proteins.game_role: Tissues with mechanical strength; larger bodies.
proteins.notes: A project summary says collagen evolved before the choanoflagellate-animal divergence; not confirmed from the primary paper.

proteins.name: Animal voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav)
proteins.function: Fast action potentials
proteins.game_role: Excitable cells and fast signalling (nerves later).
proteins.notes: Zakon: Nav evolved from Ca2+ channels and was present in the choanoflagellate-animal ancestor; clustering at axon initial segments ~0.5 Ga in early chordates.

proteins.name: Hemoglobin as an O2 carrier
proteins.function: O2 transport in body fluids
proteins.game_role: Unlocks O2 transport in a circulatory system.
proteins.notes: Globins outside animals are enzymes or sensors; O2 transport likely accompanied multicellular animals (globin census, 2006).

proteins.name: GLUT glucose facilitators (SLC2)
proteins.function: Facilitated glucose transport
proteins.game_role: Glucose uptake in animal-like cells (membrane_carrier_face default instance).
proteins.notes: Part of the MFS sugar porters; the SLC2 family's age was not checked (placeholder date, no source yet).

proteins.name: Monocarboxylate transporters (SLC16, MCT1)
proteins.function: H+-coupled lactate transport
proteins.game_role: Lactate transport in animal-like cells (membrane_carrier_face MCT1_lactate instance).
proteins.notes: Age not checked (placeholder date, no source yet).

features_note: A feature with a cost is bought with skill points in the window that opens when the level goes up, once its level is reached; points come from each level's survival and damage meters (content/parameters.json scoring.*) and from daughters released in the lineage (skills.points_per_offspring). 'effect' is the short text, 'explanation' the full one; 'reviewed' is set by a human who has checked the text (adapting_plan.md, Rules for content). 'requires' lists features that must be evolved first (a later colony feature needs multicellularity); 'requires_swallowed' is the number of prey cells the creature must have engulfed before it can be bought; 'excludes' lists features it closes: buying one makes the others unavailable. 'requires_food_gap_s' unlocks the feature only once the creature has gone that many seconds without touching or holding food (no packet touched or held, nothing in a vacuole): the famine it answers.
ocean_note: The open water of each level beyond the creature's surroundings, in mol/m³. Glucose 1 µM: free glucose in open water is nanomolar to low micromolar (placeholder to source); at 1 µM a level-1 cell without food starts starving within days (damage ~9% of lethal per day, measured 2026-10-12). Arrivals: see arrivals_note. Later levels copy level 1 until tuned.
